setupSteps: Check which way the machine is set. If it is a combined leg curl/leg extension unit, make sure it is in extension mode (the roller and seat positions differ by model; read the label or ask staff, as the mode-change method Not found as a general rule).
Weight stack pin. Pull the selector pin out and push it all the way into the lightest or second-lightest plate (Gym 4 finder sets). Push it in until it is seated fully; a half-in pin can slip.
Check the stack is clear. Nobody should be touching the stack from behind, and the cable should run freely.
Sit back all the way. Your back and hips should rest flat on the back pad, with your head relaxed. Sit tall.

Back pad/seat depth. Slide the back pad (or seat) so the crease behind your knees sits right at the front edge of the seat (a cue used by NFPT and others). Too far forward and the knee edge digs in; too far back and the knee slides off the seat edge.

Align the knee with the machine's pivot. The middle of your knee joint, seen from the side, should sit level with the machine's axis (the round bolt the lever arm turns on). Skelcore calls this the most important fit point; NFPT/Art of Manliness say the same (knee even with the pivot of the leg pad arm). If the knee is far ahead of or behind the pivot, the pad will slide along your shin and the knee will be pulled unevenly.

Set the roller on the lower shin, just above the ankle (NFPT; Art of Manliness; Skelcore: where the ankle flexes, not up the shin and not on the toes). The pad should be against the shin, not pressing on the ankle bones or the top of the foot.

Start angle (range limiter). Many machines have a lever or pin to set where the pad starts. Set it so your knees are bent to about 90° at the start (several guides) and so you can reach the bottom without straining. If your knee starts bent more than 90°, move the back pad forward or use the range limiter so the weight does not stretch the knee beyond your comfort.

Hands and feet. Hold the side handles lightly; feet relaxed with toes pointing up (a few sources describe flexing the ankle, but a neutral foot is fine for beginners). Note the back-pad and roller numbers for next time.

steps.title: Brace
steps.action: With the pin set and the pad on your lower shins, gently tighten your stomach and press your back into the pad.
steps.feel: Back and hips pressed into the seat.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back flat on the pad, thighs flat on the seat, knees about 90°. Front: both thighs level, knees in line with the hips.

steps.title: Straighten the knees
steps.action: Squeeze the front of your thighs and lift the pad by straightening both knees, in one smooth push.
steps.feel: Front of the thighs working; no pinch in the front of the knee.
steps.visualCheck: Side: only the lower legs move, hips stay down on the seat. Front: both legs rise together at the same height.

steps.title: Squeeze at the top
steps.action: Stop with the knees almost straight but still slightly soft (not locked), and hold briefly.
steps.feel: Strong thigh tension, weight held by the muscle, not the joint.
steps.visualCheck: Side: a small bend still visible at the knee; leg roughly in line with the thigh. Front: toes pointing up, knees not rolling out.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Let the roller come down slowly, resisting the weight, until the knees are back near 90°.
steps.feel: Thighs lengthening under control, no drop at the end.
steps.visualCheck: Side: smooth, steady lowering; the weight plates do not bang down. Front: legs lower at the same speed.

steps.title: Touch and go, not rest
steps.action: Let the stack lightly touch down (or stop just above it), then start the next rep without relaxing fully.
steps.visualCheck: Side: back still on the pad, hips still down.

steps.title: Finish
steps.action: After the last rep, lower the weight fully, let the stack rest, then lift your feet off the pad and stand up.
steps.visualCheck: Stack plates rest quietly; pin still in place for the next person (or moved back to the lightest plate if you were done).

commonMistakes.title: Setting the knee away from the machine pivot
commonMistakes.text: Setting the knee away from the machine pivot. Why: the pad slides on the shin and the knee is pulled along an uneven path. Fix: line the middle of the knee with the axle and note the seat number.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the knees hard at the top
commonMistakes.text: Locking the knees hard at the top. Why: puts the load on the joint, not the muscle (sources agree on a slight bend). Fix: stop just before straight and squeeze.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging or jerking the weight up
commonMistakes.text: Swinging or jerking the weight up. Why: momentum, a sudden pull on the front of the knee, and less muscle work (trainer guides: speed hurts, use a 2-1-2 tempo or slower). Fix: 2 seconds up, 1 second squeeze, 3 seconds down.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the weight on the way down
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the weight on the way down. Why: the lowering phase is where the knee takes the load, and the plates bang. Fix: 3 seconds down and let the stack touch gently.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the hips or arching the back
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the hips or arching the back. Why: signals the load is too heavy (inference from guides) and takes work off the thighs. Fix: reduce the weight until the back and hips stay still.

commonMistakes.title: Pad on the toes or high up the shin
commonMistakes.text: Pad on the toes or high up the shin. Why: changes the leverage; the pad can pinch the ankle or the toes or slide. Fix: roller just above the ankle (NFPT; Art of Manliness).

commonMistakes.title: Going too heavy with no hamstring help
commonMistakes.text: Going too heavy with no hamstring help. Why: unlike squats, the hamstrings hardly share the load in leg extensions, so heavy loads rest on the knee joint alone (ExRx-style and Wilk notes; sources advise not going excessively heavy). Fix: stay at 10–15 reps with about 3 reps left in the tank.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure (see Gym 10 MacDougall data for heavy lower-body lifts). Fix: breathe out as you lift.

safetyNotes: Knee pain at the front of the kneecap (patellofemoral pain), or cartilage problems: the leg extension puts more stress on the kneecap near the straight position (Steinkamp 1993). Use the short range (90–45° of knee bend), light weight, or choose the leg press. Stop if kneecap pain rises during or the day after.

ACL injury or after ACL surgery: do not self-direct. Ask your surgeon or physiotherapist; graft strain rises near full extension and with load (Beynnon; Escamilla 1998). Many protocols start open-chain work in limited range and progress over weeks.
Lower back problems: the back is supported, which many people find comfortable, but do not arch the back or lift the hips.

High blood pressure / heart disease: breathe out on every lift, no sets to failure, moderate loads. Do not lift if resting BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher; get clearance at 140–179/90–119 (secondary ACSM-aligned sources).

Pregnancy: the seated, upright version is generally comfortable; reduce load, no breath-holding, ask your obstetrician (ACOG supports continued strength training for healthy pregnancies; leg-extension-specific advice Not found).
Recent knee or hip surgery: follow your surgeon's limits on range and load.
Larger bodies: check the machine's maximum user weight and that the seat and back pad fit; mid-thigh pad pressure can be uncomfortable (comfort advice, est.).
